nameStory: The fragrant flatsedge gets its name from the sweet, pleasant scent that wafts from its flower clusters when crushed or brushed against. The 'flatsedge' part comes from its triangular stems that are flattened on the sides, unlike the round stems of true grasses. It's sometimes called rusty flatsedge too, referring to the reddish-brown color that develops in its seed heads as they mature.
description: Fragrant flatsedge is a grass-like plant that's actually a sedge, not a true grass. It grows in clumps up to 3 feet tall with distinctive three-sided stems and narrow, blade-like leaves. The plant produces umbrella-shaped clusters of small, brownish flowers at the top of its stems. Despite looking delicate, it's quite hardy and can pop up in disturbed areas, wet spots, and even between sidewalk cracks.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Feel the stem between your fingers - it's distinctly three-sided or triangular, not round like grass stems. The edges are sharp enough to feel but won't cut you.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny flowers cluster in umbrella-like arrangements at stem tips, starting yellowish-green and turning rusty brown. Gently crush a flower head to release a sweet, almost vanilla-like fragrance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, grass-like leaves emerge mainly from the base, with a few shorter leaves just below the flower clusters. They feel smooth and have a prominent central vein.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms loose clumps rather than spreading carpets, with individual stems standing somewhat apart from each other. Plants typically reach 1-3 feet tall.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, lens-shaped seeds that are brown to black when ripe. The seed heads persist into fall, becoming increasingly rusty-colored.

habitat: Look for fragrant flatsedge in moist, disturbed soils throughout New England, especially along pond edges, ditches, and wet meadows. It thrives in areas with periodic flooding or consistent moisture. You'll also find it in urban settings like parking lot edges and poorly drained lawns.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from the base as triangular stems. Young plants are bright green and tender, making the three-sided stem easier to feel.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering period with umbrella-shaped flower clusters appearing. This is when the fragrant scent is strongest when flowers are disturbed.
seasonality.fall: Seed heads turn distinctly rusty-brown and remain fragrant when crushed. Seeds ripen and disperse, while stems begin to yellow.
seasonality.winter: Most above-ground parts die back, but dried seed heads may persist. The plant survives underground to regrow next spring.

funFact: This plant is like nature's air freshener - indigenous peoples and early settlers would sometimes scatter the crushed flowers in their homes to create a pleasant, sweet aroma that could last for days.
confusionNotes: It's easily confused with grasses until you feel the stem - remember 'sedges have edges' while grasses have round stems. The triangular stem you can feel between your fingers is the instant giveaway that you're looking at a sedge, not a grass.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'sedge,' beginners often assume this is a grass because of its appearance. The sedge family is actually quite different from the grass family, though they look similar. Sedges are more closely related to rushes than to true grasses.
compareHints: Among New England's flatsedges, fragrant flatsedge is distinguished by its sweet scent when crushed and its preference for consistently moist soils. Yellow nutsedge tends to be more upright and grows from underground tubers, while straw-colored flatsedge is typically taller and lacks the distinctive fragrance. The umbrella-shaped flower clusters are larger and more open than those of most other flatsedges in our region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many flatsedge species, straw-colored flatsedge stands out for its relatively tall height and branching, airy flower clusters.

Among New England's flatsedges, yellow nutsedge is distinctive for its bright golden-yellow flowers and robust growth habit - most other flatsedges have brownish or straw-colored flowers and are generally smaller.
Among New England's flatsedges, toothed flatsedge is unique in reliably producing bulblets, which sets it apart from relatives like yellow nutsedge or straw-colored flatsedge.
Among its flatsedge relatives, shining flatsedge stands out for its particularly glossy flower scales - most other Cyperus species have duller, more matte-colored scales.

Among New England's many flatsedges, Great Plains flatsedge is distinguished by its compact, clumping growth habit and relatively small size compared to the taller, more sprawling straw-colored flatsedge.
Among New England's flatsedges, bearded flatsedge is distinguished by its prominently bristly flower clusters that truly look bearded.
Among its many flatsedge cousins in New England, redroot flatsedge stands alone with those brilliant red roots - no other Cyperus species has this feature.

Among New England's flatsedges, Engelmann's is distinguished by its relatively small size and compact flower clusters compared to the much taller straw-colored flatsedge or the more robust yellow nutsedge.
Among New England's flatsedges, umbrella flatsedge stays notably short and compact compared to the much taller straw-colored flatsedge or yellow nutsedge.
Among its flatsedge relatives, small-flower halfchaff sedge is distinguished by its particularly tiny flower clusters and more delicate build.
Among New England's flatsedges, Gray's is distinguished by its relatively large size and the specific arrangement of its flower clusters.
Asian flatsedge is smaller and more delicate than most of its flatsedge relatives like straw-colored flatsedge or yellow nutsedge.
Among New England's many flatsedges, fern flatsedge stands out for its particularly delicate, finely-branched flower clusters that are more lacy and open than most relatives.

Among New England's flatsedges, variable flatsedge is distinguished by its very compact, ball-like flower clusters rather than the loose, umbrella-shaped arrangements of umbrella flatsedge or the elongated spikes of yellow nutsedge.
Among New England's flatsedges, brown flatsedge is distinguished by its rich chocolate-brown flower clusters - most other flatsedges have yellow, straw-colored, or greenish flowers.
Rice flat-sedge is smaller and more delicate than most of its flatsedge relatives in New England, such as the much taller straw-colored flatsedge or the robust yellow nutsedge.
Among its flatsedge relatives, Houghton's Umbrella-sedge is distinguished by its small size and preference for sandy lake shores rather than muddy wetlands.
Yellow flatsedge is much smaller and more delicate than its relatives like yellow nutsedge, which has underground tubers, or straw-colored flatsedge, which grows much taller.
Among its flatsedge relatives, Asiatic greenhead sedge is notably smaller and more compact than yellow nutsedge or straw-colored flatsedge.
Among New England's flatsedges, Globe Flatsedge stands out for its perfectly round, compact flower clusters - most others like Yellow Nutsedge have more open, branched arrangements.
Japanese flatsedge is generally smaller and more compact than the common yellow flatsedge, and lacks the distinctive straw-colored appearance of straw-colored flatsedge.
Pinebarren flatsedge is shorter and has cylindrical flower clusters compared to most of its flatsedge relatives.
